Kiliya Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kiliya, Ukraine

Not demolished. Existing since the early 19th century, this cemetery was vandalized during WWII and again between 1945-1981; the local Jewish community restored it and fixed the gate in the 1990s, and it remains operational today. Kiliya's Jewish population numbered 249 in 1827, reaching 2,153 (19%) by 1897; 19th-century Jews were active in trade and handicrafts. By 1910, two Jewish vocational schools for men, four synagogues, and a cemetery operated, with population peaking that year at 3,018 (20%). A 1917 pogrom struck the community; a 1931 Hebrew Tarbut school and kindergarten served Jewish youth, supported by sports groups, a library, drama classes, and a Maccabi brass orchestra. Zionist organizations enabled about 50 families and chaluzim to emigrate to Palestine before WWII. Most of Kiliya's Jewish population was murdered by Romanian forces in late July 1941; 281 local Jews were interned in August 1941, deported to Transnistria that October. A Hesed branch operated in 1990, alongside the old cemetery; by 2002, 50 Jews remained in Kiliya. Notable native son microbiologist and epidemiologist Fridrich Grinbaum (1896-1961) came from the town.
